```{asis, echo = as.logical(params$showIntro)}
# Introduction

Metabolomics involves the comprehensive analysis of low-molecular-weight metabolites in biological systems. Three widely used analytical strategies address different research questions and applications:

**Untargeted assay** (also called untargeted or global metabolomics) aims to reproducibly measure as many metabolites as feasible. It generally provides relative or semiquantitative abundance data rather than absolute concentrations, and metabolite identities are not necessarily known before data acquisition.

**Targeted assay** focuses on a defined set of metabolites whose identities are known before data acquisition. With appropriate calibration and standards, it can provide absolute concentrations.

**Semitargeted assay** (often called metabolic profiling) lies between untargeted and targeted analysis. It measures a broader predefined set of metabolites and commonly reports relative or semiquantitative abundance.

This report provides an overview of your data-analysis results. Brief explanations in each section help with interpretation. A few usage tips follow.

> <span style = "color : #FF8300">**Tips:**</span>
>
> (1) Tables and selected figures are interactive, allowing you to search, zoom, pan, or inspect details. Other figures are static to ensure compatibility in a self-contained report.
>
> (2) Publication-quality static figures can be downloaded at 600 dpi from the `Statistics` page in **MetaboReport**.
>
> (3) To perform additional analyses, use the download controls above the statistical tables to export data in CSV or Excel format.
```

# Results

## Quality Control

> <span style = "color : #FF8300">**Note:**</span>
>
> If your project does not contain QC samples, you can skip this section.

Robust and reproducible data are essential for high-quality analytical results. This is particularly important in large-scale metabolomics studies, where detector-sensitivity drift and shifts in retention time or mass accuracy may occur. Raw data should therefore be inspected before processing to detect measurement bias and assess system consistency [2].

Quality-control (QC) procedures are routinely used to monitor, evaluate, and correct analytical variation in metabolomics studies. Common QC materials include pooled QC samples, reference materials, standard reference materials, and long-term reference (LTR) samples.

### PCA-based QC Evaluation

A rapid initial check can be made by performing principal component analysis (PCA) on the complete dataset. When QC samples are present, inspect their distribution in the PCA score plot in the Statistical Results section.

Ideally, QC samples should cluster tightly relative to the overall variance in the projection. Pooled QC samples often lie near the center of the PCA score plot when they represent the average composition of the biological samples. Deviations may reflect sample-preparation or analytical variation, or a pooled QC that does not represent all biological samples.

Tight QC clustering supports good analytical reproducibility, but it should be interpreted together with other QC metrics before drawing conclusions about overall data quality [1].

### Comprehensive QC Report

You may also receive an HTML QC report generated with the R package **RawHummus**, which evaluates metabolomics data quality using QC samples. `RawHummus` uses 12 quality metrics related to liquid chromatography (LC) peak shape, retention time (RT), mass accuracy, detector sensitivity, and fragmentation [2].

> <span style = "color : #FF8300">**Note:**</span>
>
> A detailed evaluation of data quality can be found in the RawHummus report.
>
> The RawHummus report may be suitable as supplementary material, subject to journal requirements.
>
> Please cite the RawHummus publication in your manuscript [2].


## Statistical Results

### PCA

Principal component analysis (PCA) is an unsupervised method that transforms correlated variables into linearly uncorrelated variables called `principal components`. The first component explains as much variation as possible, and each subsequent component explains the greatest remaining variation. PCA helps reduce dimensionality and visualize the structure of the data.

PCA scores describe the position of each sample along the principal components. Scores are commonly plotted in two dimensions, usually PC1 versus PC2. Each point represents a sample: nearby samples have more similar multivariate profiles, whereas distant samples are more dissimilar. Coloring points by sample type helps assess QC consistency and identify potential sample outliers.


```{r}
#| label = PCA,
#| echo = FALSE,
#| warning = FALSE,

#(2) show PCA plot--------------------------------------------------------------

params$myPCAPlot
```

> <span style = "color : #FF8300">**Note:**</span>
>
> This PCA score plot provides an overview of the data structure, helps identify potential outliers, and—when QC samples are present—supports evaluation of analytical reproducibility.

### Clustered Heatmap

A clustered heatmap represents values on a color scale. Clustering samples and mass features can reveal groups with coordinated patterns. The rows of the heatmap below represent samples, and the columns represent mass features.


```{r}
#| label = CompleteHeatmap,
#| echo = FALSE,
#| warning = FALSE,
#| message = FALSE,
#| out.width = "100%"
#(2) show heatmap plot----------------------------------------------------------

params$myHMPlot
```

> <span style = "color : #FF8300">**Note:**</span>
>
> Depending on the settings used in the **MetaboReport** workflow, the heatmap may include all detected mass features or only statistically significant features.
>
> 1. A heatmap constructed with all mass features (or metabolites) provides an overview of the data structure.
>
> 2. A heatmap constructed with selected differential mass features (or metabolites) can make sample-group differences easier to visualize.

> <span style = "color : #FF8300">**How to interpret Table 1?**</span>
>
> **(1) Parameters in Table 1**
>
> `Fold_X_vs_Y`: Fold change (FC) between Group X and Group Y. It is defined as the ratio X/Y and describes the relative change in a metabolite or mass feature between the groups.
>
> `AdjPvalue_X_vs_Y`: Adjusted p-value for the comparison between Group X and Group Y.
>
> `VIP_X_vs_Y`: Variable importance in projection for Group X versus Group Y. This metric is derived from the OPLS-DA model. See the OPLS-DA section for details.
>
> **(2) How to perform feature selection?**
>
> In metabolomics, feature selection can identify metabolites or mass features that help distinguish Group X from Group Y (for example, wild-type and mutant groups).
>
> You can combine `FC`, adjusted p-value, and `VIP` to select differential-feature candidates from the statistical results in Table 1.
>
> The summary below uses adjusted p-value < 0.05 and VIP > 1, with FC >= 2 classified as increased and FC <= 0.5 classified as decreased.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Differential Features

**Table 2. Summary of statistical results**

The following criteria are used to select differential mass-feature or metabolite candidates:

Candidates must have an adjusted **p-value < 0.05** and **VIP > 1**. Among these candidates, **FC >= 2** indicates an increase and **FC <= 0.5** indicates a decrease.

```{r}
#| label = summary,
#| echo = FALSE,
#| warning = FALSE,
#| message = FALSE,
#| out.width = "100%"

## extract group information
GroupInfo <- myStat %>%
  dplyr::select(starts_with("AdjPvalue")) %>%
  colnames() %>%
  gsub(pattern = "AdjPvalue_", replacement = "")

## prepare the table
statSummary <- data.frame(matrix(0, ncol = 3, nrow = length(GroupInfo))) %>%
  dplyr::rename("Increase (FC >= 2)" = X1, "Decrease (FC <= 0.5)" = X2, "Total" = X3) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(Group = GroupInfo) %>%
  dplyr::relocate(Group)

## get summary
for (i in seq_along(GroupInfo)) {
  dfIndex <- statSummary$Group[i]
  filteredStat <- myStat %>%
    dplyr::select(contains(dfIndex)) %>%
    dplyr::filter(!!sym(paste0("AdjPvalue_", dfIndex)) < 0.05) %>%
    dplyr::filter(!!sym(paste0("VIP_", dfIndex)) > 1)
  statSummary[i, 2] <- filteredStat %>%
    dplyr::filter(!!sym(paste0("Fold_", dfIndex)) >= 2) %>%
    dplyr::count() %>%
    as.numeric()
  statSummary[i, 3] <- filteredStat %>%
    dplyr::filter(!!sym(paste0("Fold_", dfIndex)) <= 0.5) %>%
    dplyr::count() %>%
    as.numeric()
  statSummary[i, 4] <- statSummary[i, 2] + statSummary[i, 3]
  }

DT::datatable(statSummary,
              extensions = 'Buttons',
              options = list(scrollX = TRUE,
                             deferRender = TRUE,
                             scroller = TRUE,
                             fixedColumns = FALSE,
                             ## add download options
                             dom = 'Bfrtip',
                             buttons = list('print',
                                            list(extend = 'collection',
                                                 buttons = c('csv', 'excel'),
                                                 text = 'Download'
                                                 )
                                             ),
                             ## customize header
                               initComplete = DT::JS(
                                 "function(settings, json) {",
                                 "$(this.api().table().header()).css({'background-color': '#98be98', 'color': '#fff'});",
                                "}")
                              )
               )
```

### OPLS-DA

Orthogonal partial least squares discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA) is a supervised method that separates predictive variation related to class membership from orthogonal variation unrelated to class separation. Because supervised models can overfit, interpret them together with cross-validation and permutation-test results rather than relying on visual separation alone.

R2Y describes model fit, whereas Q2 estimates predictive performance. A high R2Y combined with a much lower Q2 can indicate overfitting. Permutation-test results (pR2Y and pQ2) provide additional evidence when assessing model validity [3].

The `S-plot` combines modeled covariance (x-axis) and modeled correlation (y-axis) from OPLS-DA. Features with large absolute covariance and correlation, together with VIP >= 1, may contribute strongly to group separation and should be evaluated with supporting statistical and biological evidence.

```{r}
#| label = OPLSDA,
#| echo = FALSE,
#| warning = FALSE,
#| message = FALSE,
#| out.width = '100%'
#(6) show OPLSDA result---------------------------------------------------------

## prepare data
OPLSDALevel <- sampleGroup[, OPLSDAGroup]
listnames <- report_group_pairs(OPLSDALevel)

if (!length(listnames)) {
  cat("OPLS-DA requires at least two non-QC groups.\n\n")
}

## plot
for (i in seq_along(listnames)){
  dfOPLSDA <- cbind.data.frame(dataGlobal3PCA, Group = sampleGroup[, OPLSDAGroup]) %>%
    dplyr::filter(Group %in% listnames[[i]])
  matrixOPLSDA <- dplyr::select(dfOPLSDA, -Group)
  groupOPLSDA <- as.factor(dfOPLSDA$Group)

  ## perform OPLSDA
  resultOPLSDA <- tryCatch(
    ropls::opls(
      matrixOPLSDA,
      groupOPLSDA,
      log10L = FALSE,
      scaleC = "none",
      predI = 1,
      permI = 20,
      orthoI = 1,
      crossvalI = min(length(groupOPLSDA), 7),
      fig.pdfC = "none",
      info.txtC = "none"
    ),
    error = function(error) NULL
  )

  if (is.null(resultOPLSDA)) {
    cat("An OPLS-DA model could not be fitted for ",
        paste(listnames[[i]], collapse = " versus "), ".\n\n", sep = "")
    next
  }

  # Keep these as ggplot objects. plotly 4.10.x cannot convert ggplot2 4.x
  # objects and aborts the entire report with "subscript out of bounds".
  p1 <- showOPLSDA(resultOPLSDA, Group = groupOPLSDA, size = 1, interactive = FALSE)
  p2 <- showSplot(matrixOPLSDA, resultOPLSDA, size = 1, interactive = FALSE)
  print(p1)
  print(p2)
}
```

### Volcano Plot

```{r}
#| label = volcanoPlot,
#| echo = FALSE,
#| warning = FALSE,
#| message = FALSE
#(6) show volcano plot result---------------------------------------------------

## The code is used to generate a list of volcano plots
VCGroupLevel <- sampleGroup[, VCGroup]
listnames <- report_group_pairs(VCGroupLevel)

if (!length(listnames)) {
  cat("Volcano plots require at least two non-QC groups.\n\n")
}
for (i in seq_along(listnames)){
  volcanoPlot <- showVolcano(
    result = statTable,
    compare_group = listnames[[i]],
    FC = 2,
    pValue = 0.05,
    interactive = FALSE
  )
  print(volcanoPlot)
}
```

### K-means Cluster Analysis

K-means cluster analysis can reveal subsets of mass features that display different profiles across sample groups.

The cluster plot shows the profile pattern of each subset.

The table provides details for each feature, including the metabolite name (when available), standardized peak area, and group information.

### Bar Plot

The bar plot summarizes each selected metabolite across sample groups.

> <span style = "color : #FF8300">**Note:**</span>
>
> The transformation selected in the **MetaboReport** workflow is applied before plotting. Refer to the y-axis label for the transformation method.
>
> Select a metabolite to update both the plot and its corresponding table.


```{r}
#| label = BoxPlot,
#| echo = FALSE,
#| warning = FALSE,
#| message = FALSE,
#| out.width = '100%'
#(8) show box plot result-------------------------------------------------------
BPData <- dataGlobal3Transform %>%
  dplyr::mutate(Group = sampleGroup[, BPGroup]) %>%
  dplyr::filter(Group != "QC") %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(!Group, names_to = "Metabolite", values_to = "Area") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(Area = round(Area, 2)) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(Metabolite, Group) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(MEAN = round(mean(Area), 2), SD = round(sd(Area), 2))

## must order data by the colored variable here to avoid mismatch of standard deviation.
## See issue 15
BPData <- BPData[order(BPData$Group), ]
BPColors <- nature_palette(length(unique(BPData$Group)))
BPData <- crosstalk::SharedData$new(BPData)
metaboliteFilter <- crosstalk::filter_select(id = "Metabolite",
                                             label = "Select a metabolite",
                                             sharedData = BPData,
                                             group = ~ Metabolite,
                                             multiple = FALSE
                                             )
yLegend <- switch(params$BPTransform,
                  none = "Raw Peak Area",
                  log2 = "Log2-transformed Peak Area",
                  log10 = "Log10-transformed Peak Area"
                  )

BPPlot <- plotly::plot_ly(data = BPData,
                          x = ~ Group,
                          y = ~ MEAN,
                          color = ~ Group,
                          colors = BPColors,
                          marker = list(line = list(color = 'grey', width = 1.5)),
                          error_y = ~list(array = SD, color = 'grey'),
                          type = 'bar'
                          ) %>%
  plotly::layout(yaxis = list(categoryorder = "trace", title = yLegend)) %>%
  plotly::config(toImageButtonOptions = list(format = "svg", filename = "plot"))

filter <- crosstalk::bscols(
  metaboliteFilter,
  BPPlot,
  widths = 12
  )

crosstalk::bscols(filter)
```
